title: Is AI About to Revolutionise the Classroom? Technology Ashman, Greg
author: Ashman, Greg
summary: Ashman, a skeptic and heavy AI user himself, examines whether generative AI will finally transform education by critiquing the Alpha School '2 Hour Learning' model and comparing it to a childhood memory of laminated-card mathematics instruction that also promised personalized learning and also failed to spread. He runs the historical pattern: interactive CD-ROMs, multimedia learning research, Google -- each was 'different' in the same way AI is now claimed to be different, and none transformed education. The central argument is that media debates miss the real problem: acquiring biologically secondary knowledge (reading, writing, mathematics) is intrinsically unmotivating because humans have not evolved mechanisms to seek it out, and history shows that neither engaging visuals nor pseudo-intelligent software has solved the motivational problem. The commercial evidence from Khanmigo's retirement suggests that even when given the option, humans choose not to engage AI. Ashman closes with genuine agnosticism: 'I'll wait and see.'
points: The Alpha School '2 Hour Learning' model -- AI-delivered personalized instruction with teachers as guides -- closely resembles the laminated-card individualized mathematics instruction Ashman experienced as a child, which also never spread despite promising the same benefits.

The historical pattern of educational technology (film, television, Papert's turtles, CD-ROMs, Google, interactive whiteboards) is consistent: each was claimed to be transformative, each generated research, and none fundamentally changed how students learn at scale.

The central problem AI shares with all previous media is not interactivity but motivation: biologically secondary knowledge (reading, writing, math) is intrinsically a hard slog because humans have not evolved to seek it out, and medium changes have not solved this.

Commercial evidence that humans prefer not to engage AI voluntarily -- the retirement of Khanmigo after users declined to use it when given the choice -- challenges the AI-in-education optimists' implicit assumption that students will consistently choose to engage.

The medium of instruction is largely agnostic in its effects: what matters is not whether you project a booklet page or a PowerPoint slide but what you do with the medium -- and AI is another medium, not an answer to the motivational problem at the heart of schooling.
quotes: Just as laminated cards did not transform mathematics teaching, silent reading, where students all read different books while the teacher guides and motivates them, has not transformed reading instruction. Similarly, the advent of film, television and Seymour Papert and his turtles did not transform education very much.

Interestingly, there is some commercial evidence that when given the option, humans will choose not to interact with AI, as Dan Meyer's essay about the retirement of Khanmigo, Khan Academy's AI assistant, demonstrates.

We seem to have created schools to pass on, at scale, what David C Geary has termed 'biologically secondary knowledge'. This is knowledge that has been created relatively recently, such as how to read and write, or how to solve quadratic equations.
Reading, writing, mathematics and, by extension, the whole academic curriculum, are a hard slog. We are not naturally motivated by any of it. If motivation comes at all, it comes later.

We might assume that engaging visuals or a pseudo-intelligent computer program would help children over the motivational hump, but history tells us otherwise. It takes far more -- external motivators that gradually transition to internal motivators as capabilities incrementally increase.
I am agnostic about the medium of instruction. I don't think it makes much difference. It's not the medium of video that matters but what you do with it. Arguments about media miss the point.
